title: the sounds
hook: a word said wrong at a family puja, and two old stories about whether it matters
tomorrow: when a nervous voice shakes, why would anyone start with a hum?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sounds held a puzzle: an r that is a vowel, hiding in Krishna's name, said ri in some mouths and ru in others. Which raises a fair question: how much does the saying matter?

A wedding toast, a name read at graduation, a line said at a family puja: someone gets a word wrong, and the room splits. Half wince. Half say, relax, they meant well. Hindu tradition has this argument too, with a story for each side. Here's the first. Tvashtr, a craftsman god, wants a son who will kill Indra. He pours the offering and calls out the son's name: indrashatru. But he puts the accent in the wrong place. Said one way, the word means slayer of Indra. Said his way, it means the one whose slayer is Indra. And that is how the story ends.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS IT WRONG.` → `TVASHTR CALLS OUT A NAME.` → `THE ACCENT FLIPS THE MEANING.`

segments.voice: The Paniniya Shiksha, an old manual on sounds, turns that story into a warning. A mantra said with a wrong sound or a wrong accent doesn't say what it means, and can even turn on the one who says it, the way indrashatru did. On this side stand the chanters who give years to getting every syllable right. Their best case: these words were handed down by ear, one mouth to the next. Small carelessness, repeated over generations, would wear a verse away. Exactness is a form of care. Now the other story. In a telling found in the Adhyatma Ramayana, a robber who will one day be the sage Valmiki can't bring himself to say Rama's name. So sages give it to him backwards: mara, mara. Said over and over, mara mara runs together into rama rama. Tradition says he repeated it until an anthill grew over him. On this side stand the devotees who say the name with love, accent or no accent. Their best case: God isn't fooled by a mouth, and a name said with a whole heart reaches where it's meant to go. The tradition holds both. Vedic chanters keep the first for the Vedas. Bhakti singers keep the second for the name. And some keep both at once: care with the sound, and the heart behind it.
screen: `A WRONG SOUND SAYS THE WRONG THING.` · `EXACTNESS IS A FORM OF CARE.` · `MARA, MARA, BECOMES RAMA.` · `A WHOLE HEART IS HEARD.` · then, large: `THE TRADITION HOLDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Write one name you love by hand, slowly, every letter where it belongs. Then read it once, quietly, with the person it belongs to in mind. Care with the sound, and the heart behind it, in one small act.
The sounds: today, two old answers to whether they must be exact. The chanter's care, and the devotee's heart.
For the road: the sounds, guarded by the chanter's care and carried by the devotee's heart. That's today.

howItsDone: Vedic chanters train for years to keep every syllable and accent exact, while bhakti traditions sing and repeat the names of God in many accents and languages; some families hold both in the same home.

fork.setup: at a family puja your uncle says a line of Sanskrit with the accents all over the place. you lean toward the heart side. what's the best case for the other side?
options: words handed down by ear would wear away if no one guarded each sound.
God hears only perfect Sanskrit, so the whole puja doesn't count now.

fork.reveal: the chanters' case is care: the Shiksha warns a wrong sound can say the wrong thing, as indrashatru did. a fair steelman keeps that case at its strongest, not its harshest.

original.note: Sanskrit: indraśatru. Accented one way, slayer of Indra; the other way, the one whose slayer is Indra.

options: both views live in the tradition: care for the sound, and the heart.
your cousin: a wrong sound cancels the line, whatever you meant.

chat.meaning: The Shiksha guards every sound; the mara-to-rama story trusts the heart. Both are inside Hinduism, and some people keep both.

Tvashtr.meaning: a craftsman god in the Vedic stories

Indra.meaning: the Vedic king of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt

Adhyatma Ramayana.meaning: a devotional retelling of Rama's story
